bib.title: No More Manual Tests? Evaluating and Improving ChatGPT for Unit Test Generation

legacy_report:
I read all 24 pages of Yuan et al. (ChatTester). It fits **05-verification-loops.md**. Its compile-error repair loop is a worked example for "Feed the error back as context" and "Retry taxonomy". Its stopping rule (quit after too many rounds that don't reduce the error count) fits "Loop detection" and "Failure, recovery, and termination". It doesn't fit 10-scope-and-done.md well. The paper's one point about deciding when a test is "done" is that a test that compiles is not a test that passes, and 05 already makes that point.

Answers to your three questions:
- **Compile and pass rates:** with a basic prompt, 42.1% of ChatGPT's tests compile and 24.8% pass.
- **Wrong assertions:** 85.5% of the tests that compile but fail, fail on an assertion. The authors checked by hand and every one was a wrong assertion, not a real bug.
- **The repair loop:** on its own it lifts compilation from 39.0% to 60.6% and passing from 22.3% to 34.0%. With the intention prompt added, it adds 22.6 points of compilation and 11.3 points of passing.

```text
SOURCE: "No More Manual Tests? Evaluating and Improving ChatGPT for Unit Test Generation", Zhiqiang Yuan, Mingwei Liu, Shiji Ding, Kaixin Wang, Yixuan Chen, Xin Peng, Yiling Lou (Fudan University). Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 1, FSE, Article 76 (FSE 2024), July 2024; arXiv 2305.04207v3 (19 May 2024). First posted 2023.

COVERAGE: 89,148 of 89,148 chars; 24 of 24 pages. All body text, tables, threats to validity and references read. There are no appendices. References skimmed for where the method comes from.

CLAIMS
- claim: With a basic prompt, about two in five ChatGPT tests compile and about one in four pass.
  number: 42.1% compile; 24.8% pass (Evosuite 97.6 / 91.4; AthenaTest 18.8 / 14.4)
  setup: gpt-3.5-turbo through the API with default settings, one zero-shot prompt (role line + task line + focal method, class name, fields, method signatures). 1,000 Java focal methods drawn from 185 Maven projects (CodeSearchNet, ≥100 stars, updated since 2023-01-01). JUnit. The test is placed in the focal class's directory, then compiled and run. One run, not repeated.
  quote: "42.1% of the generated tests are successfully compiled while only 24.8% of the generated tests are executed successfully without any execution errors"
  where: p.8, Table 2
- claim: Most failures come before execution. 57.9% don't compile, and 17.3% compile but fail, mostly on wrong assertions.
  number: 57.9% / 17.3%
  setup: as above
  quote: "57.9% of ChatGPT-generated tests encounter compilation errors, such as using undefined symbols, violating type constraints, or accessing private fields; and 17.3% of the tests are compilable but fail during execution, which mostly result from the incorrect assertions"
  where: p.3
- claim: Wrong assertions cause most execution failures. Every assertion failure checked by hand was a wrong assertion, not a real bug.
  number: 85.5% (148 assertion errors out of the failed executions in Table 4)
  setup: the 1,000-method study; failures inspected by hand
  quote: "the majority of failed executions (85.5%) are caused by assertion errors ... we find all of them as a result of incorrect assertions generated by ChatGPT"
  where: p.9-10, Table 4
- claim: Compile errors are mostly unresolved symbols (classes, methods or variables the model made up), then type errors and access to private members.
  number: "cannot find symbol class" 1,934; method 471; variable 466; incompatible types 73; private access 75; abstract instantiation 33 (counts across 579 tests that don't compile)
  setup: as above; only errors seen more than 10 times are listed
  quote: "the number of each compilation errors in 579 uncompilable tests. Note that there could be multiple compilation errors in one test"
  where: p.9, Table 3
- claim: The full ChatTester (intention prompt + compile-error repair loop) adds 34.3 points of compilation and 18.7 points of passing. These are absolute points, not relative gains.
  number: compile 39.0 → 73.3; pass 22.3 → 41.0
  setup: a separate set of 100 focal methods (from the 748 left over), gpt-3.5-turbo, each run 3 times and averaged
  quote: "additional 34.3% tests (= 73.3% - 39.0%) can be successfully compiled and additional 18.7% tests (= 41.0% - 22.3%) can pass the execution"
  where: p.17, Table 7
- claim: Ablation. The repair loop alone does more than the intention prompt alone, and adding the loop on top of the intention prompt gives a further 22.6 points of compilation and 11.3 of passing.
  number: Ite (no loop) 50.7 / 29.7; Ini (loop only) 60.6 / 34.0; full 73.3 / 41.0
  setup: as above
  quote: "additional 22.6% tests and 11.3% tests are fixed by the iterative test refiner into compilable tests and passing tests"
  where: p.17, Table 7
- claim: Asking the model first for the method's intention fixes some wrong assertions.
  number: 12.5% of incorrect-assertion tests fixed; +11.7 points compile, +7.4 points pass
  setup: ChatTester-Ite against basic ChatGPT, 100-method set
  quote: "among the ChatGPT-generated tests with incorrect assertions, 12.5% of them are fixed into correct assertions in ChatTester-Ite"
  where: p.17
- claim: Late repair rounds produce tests that compile but don't pass. In Table 8, every passing test is in rounds 0-2, while rounds 6-7 still add compiling tests (15 and 6). The authors don't draw this conclusion; it is read straight from the table.
  number: passing by round 31, 9, 2, then 0; compiling at round 6 = 15
  setup: Table 8, 100 tests
  quote: "# Passing Execution 31 9 2 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0"
  where: p.17, Table 8
- claim: The loop's stopping rule. Stop when the test compiles. A round counts as invalid if the error count doesn't fall, and the loop stops after 3 invalid rounds.
  number: 3
  setup: ChatTester controller design
  quote: "if the number of compilation errors is larger than or the same as that in the last iteration, the current refinement is considered an invalid refinement. The controller would terminate the refinement if the accumulated number of invalid refinements is larger than the maximum (e.g., 3 in our experiments)"
  where: p.15
- claim: Cost. Each test takes about 99 s on average, and each repair round about 30 s.
  number: 99.0 s total; 15.0 s initial; 30.0 s per round; about 10 s API latency
  setup: gpt-3.5-turbo API, compiling the whole project each round
  quote: "The average time cost of ChatTester is around 99.0 seconds, where the initial test generator takes 15.0 seconds while each iteration in the iterative refiner takes 30.0 seconds on average"
  where: p.17
- claim: The same approach helps open-source 34B models, which start from far lower baselines.
  number: CodeLlama-34B compile 22 → 43, pass 3 → 21; CodeFuse-34B compile 1 → 24, pass 0 → 11; time 5 s → 105 s / 90 s
  setup: CodeLlama-Instruct-34B and CodeFuse-34B on the 100-method set
  quote: "ChatTester achieves 21.0%/ 23.0% improvement in compilation rate and 11.0% /18.0% improvement in passing execution rate"
  where: p.18, Table 9
- claim: Tests that pass match hand-written ones on coverage of the focal method.
  number: statement 82.3 against 84.2 manual; branch 65.6 against 68.9
  setup: only focal methods where both ChatGPT and Evosuite produced tests that run
  quote: "Statement 82.3 65.5 68.0 39.7 76.2 56.9 81.1 84.2"
  where: p.10, Table 5
- claim: On Python the repair loop gives a smaller gain.
  number: 31.7% → 43.2% pass
  setup: 164 HumanEval problems
  quote: "improving the successful execution rate of ChatGPT-generated tests from 31.7% to 43.2%"
  where: p.19
- claim: Whole-project coverage beats basic ChatGPT and is roughly level with Evosuite.
  number: zappos-json statement coverage: ChatTester 35.1, Evosuite 30.5, ChatGPT 14.4
  setup: 3 projects of 3.5k-6.3k LOC
  quote: "ChatTester 35.1 21.5 15.6 9.2 41.8 13.4"
  where: p.18, Table 10

LIMITS: The repair loop only fixes compile errors. Execution failures are left alone because "it is challenging to identify whether a test execution failure is caused by the incorrect test code or by the incorrect focal method" (p.15). So the loop can't catch the wrong-assertion failure mode. The empirical study ran once ("We do not repeat our experiments in the empirical study"); only the ChatTester evaluation averages 3 runs. The ChatTester results rest on 100 methods. The user study had 5 participants with 4-5 years of experience each, paid $250 each. Only single-test-case methods were kept, and only Maven Java projects, chosen by name and path matching. There is a training-data leakage risk, which the authors address only through edit distance ("only 5% ... less than 200-characters Levenshtein distance"). The model is gpt-3.5-turbo, not GPT-4, so the absolute rates are dated. Evosuite's higher correctness comes from filtering after generation, and the authors say they "do not intend to conclude that Evosuite is better". AthenaTest was rebuilt by the authors on CodeT5, not the original model.

BUILDS ON: Tufano et al. 2020 (AthenaTest; also the code context included in the prompt); Watson et al. 2020 (learning assertions); Nie et al. 2023 (TeCo; also the correctness metrics); Fraser & Arcuri 2011 (EvoSuite); Barr et al. 2015 (the oracle problem; splitting a test into prefix and oracle); Husain et al. 2019 (CodeSearchNet project list); Wei et al. 2022 (chain of thought) and Yao et al. 2023 (tree of thoughts), credited as the ideas behind breaking the task into steps; Pacheco et al. 2007 (feedback-directed random testing). Related work it contrasts with: CodaMosa (Lemieux et al. 2023), LIBRO (Kang et al. 2023), TestPilot (Schäfer et al. 2024), Ring (Joshi et al. 2023).

CODE: No code listings are in the text. Prompt wording, verbatim from p.6: "You are a professional who writes Java test methods." and "Please write a test method for the {focal method name} based on the given information using {Junit version}". Code repository: https://github.com/FudanSELab/ChatTester/tree/main (ref [12]).

FIGURES:
- Fig. 7, p.13, "The Workflow of ChatTester": the generator → compile → error-message parser → code analyzer → re-prompt loop on one page. Best fit for 05.
- Fig. 9, p.14, "Prompt in the Iterative Test Refiner": a two-round repair showing the <Buggy line> tag and the extra class context (the Xml class) inserted into the prompt. Shows concretely what "feed the error back" means.
- Fig. 8, p.13, "Basic Prompt v.s. Prompts in the Initial Test Generator": setCharAt example where asking for the intention first corrects the assertion.
- Fig. 3, p.10, "NullPointerException Example": the model doesn't know about external resources. Minor.
- Tables 2, 7 and 8 (pp.8, 17) carry the numbers and may be better rebuilt as a small chart than shown as figures.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. The Table 9 header extracted garbled (stray math-italic model names). I read the columns as CodeLlama / CodeLlama+ChatTester / CodeFuse / CodeFuse+ChatTester, which the prose figures confirm. Table 10 has a typo, "13,3". The abstract and conclusion describe the 18.7-point gain as "18.7% more tests with correct assertions", but the body defines it as the gain in execution pass rate (41.0 − 22.3). Cite it as pass rate. All gains are percentage points, not relative increases. The meaning of each row in Table 8 is somewhat unclear (the rows add up to 100 tests).
```
